newsitem.title: MEXICO: New Year ushers in competition for Mexico's Telmex.
newsitem.headline: New Year ushers in competition for Mexico's Telmex.

text.p: After decades of complaining about poor telephone service, Mexicans finally will be able to do something about it when the country's telephone market opens its doors to competition starting New Year's Day.

U.S. telephone giants such as AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. have linked up with local partners and are among eight firms vying to beat former monopoly Telefonos de Mexico, better known as Telmex, on its own turf.
The Mexican market, now at 93 million people, has been Telmex's sole domain for half a century.

Competition at first will target the lucrative long-distance market -- a $4 billion-a-year business expected to double by the year 2000. Local service also is open to competition but probably will not attract rivals for a few years.

"Mexico is an exciting market ... and we are very bullish about what we will acheive here," said Dan Crawford, an MCI executive and president of Avantel, a joint venture between the U.S. company and Mexican financial company Grupo Financiero Banamex-Accival.
The new companies are expected to invest more than $5 billion in the next few years, probably the single largest source of foreign direct investment in Mexico this decade.

Although Telmex officially lost its monopoly in August, competitors could only place calls on networks of their own, which they just recently started to build and are in place mostly for bigger, corporate clients.

As of 1997, the law requires Telmex to hook up rivals to its giant local network, and hence to millions of customers' telephones. Telmex will get a connection fee that will decline over a few years as the new firms build their own networks.

To avoid opening the market too fast, only a handful of Mexican cities, such as Monterrey and Queretaro will kick off the process on New Year's Day Wednesday. Other cities like Mexico City will wait until April.
For Mexicans, the new companies offer a chance to get back at Telmex after decades of suffering with having lines suddenly die or being billed for calls that were never made.
As recently as three years ago, most Mexicans polled wanted the new owners of Telmex, which was sold by the government in 1990, to go to jail on corruption and mismanagement charges.
Marina Sanchez, a middle-class accountant in Mexico City, said she planned to switch to another company as soon as she can.
"For years, they gave us lousy service. They can't expect to keep our business," she said.

Avantel and other companies have played up Telmex's bad image in their television ads. Telmex itself has tacitly acknowledged it has an image problem by planning to compete in the long-distance under its brand name "Lada."
Despite their brash attitude, however, the new phone companies won't be competing against the Telmex of old.

Many here agree the phone giant has cleaned up its act since its sale to a group of investors, including billionaire Carlos Slim and minority partners San Antonio, Texas-based SBC Communications Inc. and France Telecom.

During the past six years, Telmex has invested more than $11 billion to update the country's outdated network. Phone lines that used to take months to install are now ready in days. Billing is easy and accurate.
Ahead of the competition, Telmex also has cut long-distance rates to international levels and begun offering discounts and newer services like call waiting and high-speed data lines.
"One should not underestimate the incumbent. ... Telmex is not going to be caught unprepared," said Simon Flannery, a telecommunications analyst at investment bank J.P. Morgan & Co. In. in New York.
Telmex will probably lose 30 percent to 50 percent of its market share by the year 2000, analysts say. Lower prices due to competition will also squeeze the company's margins.
Worries about competition have caused the price of Telmex stock, one of the world's most active issues, to remain flat during the past year.

But there is good news for Telmex, which will have a smaller share of a bigger telecommunications market as Mexico's economy grows and modernizes and lower prices boost telephone traffic. Analysts say the long-distance market could grow by 13 percent a year.
